newsitem.title: UK: Gold's gains on U.S.-Iraq tensions shortlived.
newsitem.headline: Gold's gains on U.S.-Iraq tensions shortlived.

text.p: Gold prices firmed on Tuesday following U.S. missile strikes on Iraq, but the gains rapidly evaporated as investors snubbed the traditional "safe haven".
"Gold reacted in the first few minutes of the attack but then the whole thing fizzled out," a dealer said.
Modest early morning gains of about $0.75 eroded during European trading, and gold closed in London at $386.95 an ounce, just five cents higher than on Monday afternoon.
Gold's role as a "safe haven" in times of turmoil and economic instability was seen unlikely to surface unless the Mid-East conflict deepened, dealers said.
"I don't think it's going to go crazy on this unless we see a severe worsening in the near future," a dealer said, pegging gold's near-term price range at $386-$388.
The United States launched 27 cruise missiles against air defence targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds in the north, the Pentagon said.
Silver followed gold higher but eased back to finish one cent lower at $5.18 an ounce. Platinum ended 25 cents firmer at $396.25, but palladium closed 25 cents lower at $125.75.
Overall, the strikes could have negative implications for gold, said Andy Smith, an analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland.
A surge in oil prices resulting from Mid-East tensions would lead to expectations of higher interest rates, which in turn would diminish gold's appeal to investors, he said.
"Central banks no longer have the luxury to play dead while oil prices rise. The market expects higher interest rates," Smith said.
Memories of the Persian Gulf war five years ago -- when gold prices soared and then collapsed -- also tempered extreme reaction in the market, dealers said.
"People remember 1991," said Anderson Cheung, chief dealer at Swiss Bank Corporation.
When Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait on August 1, 1990, the gold price jumped nearly $20 to a fix of $382.00 the following day.
The metal hit a peak of $415.70 on August 23 before slipping back. On the eve of the allied invasion to remove occupying Iraqi troops, gold climbed again to fix at $403.70.
The offensive began early on January 17, 1991 provoking a huge sell-off of gold, which fixed at $383.50 that day.
